# A sector-comparison triangle for every strict half-cap planar body

This note removes the double-core hypothesis from the boundedness portion of
`candidate fd39a28eeb41e9c4`.
The resulting triangle is a SECTOR comparison body. The original body need
not be contained in it.

## 1. Actual rays, sectors, and bridge halfplanes

Let K be a planar convex body with zero in its interior and three balanced
spanning normals. Make their common invertible linear normalization to

    v_1=(1,0), v_2=(0,1), v_3=(-1,-1).

Write its six actual boundary-ray points in cyclic order as

    P_0=(A,0), P_1=(0,B), P_2=(-t,t),
    P_3=(-a,0), P_4=(0,-b), P_5=(r,-r),

with all six scalar radii positive. The three unique sectors are between
P_5,P_0; P_1,P_2; P_3,P_4, and have areas X_1,X_2,X_3. The opposite double
sectors, missed by caps 1,2,3 respectively, have areas Y_1,Y_2,Y_3, with

    Y_1>=at/2, Y_2>=br/2, Y_3>=AB/2.                  (1)

These inequalities hold because K contains the convex hull of its ray
points and zero. Boundary rays have zero planar measure.

Define the three bridge halfplanes that contain zero by the lines through
the double-sector endpoint pairs:

    x/A+y/B<=1,
    x+(1-a/t)y>=-a,
    y+(1-b/r)x>=-b.                                  (2)

Let T be their intersection. Every ray point belongs to every halfplane in
(2). Indeed the six ray points lie on the boundary of their convex hull:
an interior point of that hull would be interior to K, contradicting its
actual boundary-ray status. In cyclic angular order the adjacent bridge
segments are boundary segments of that convex hull. Thus their inward
halfplanes contain all six points. In particular T contains the six-ray
hull and zero lies strictly inside all three halfplanes.

## 2. Local bridge constraints do not require a global support line

A point of K in any unique sector satisfies its two ADJACENT bridge
inequalities, even if those bridge lines fail to support all of K.

For example let (x,y) lie in unique sector 1, so x>=0, y<=0, x+y>=0.
If x/A+y/B>1, its segment to P_1=(0,B) crosses the positive x-axis at

    (Bx/(B-y),0),

whose first coordinate is strictly larger than A. This is a point of K
on the ray beyond its prescribed endpoint, a contradiction. Consequently
the first bridge inequality holds. The same segment argument with P_4
and the cutting ray through P_5 proves the other adjacent inequality.
The two cyclic relabelings prove the assertion in all unique sectors.
Boundary cases follow either from the same non-strict formula or by
continuity from interior points of a sector.

The NONadjacent bridge inequality automatically holds on that whole unique
cone. For unique sector 1, for example, the nonadjacent bridge joins P_2,P_3;
its normal points oppositely to every ray in unique cone 1. Explicitly its
left side is x+(1-a/t)y=(x+y)-(a/t)y>=0>-a. The cyclic versions are identical.
Hence

    K intersect unique sector i
        subset T intersect unique sector i             (3)

for every i. This is local sector containment, not K subset T.

## 3. Strict half caps force T to be bounded

Assume all three cap areas Q_i=|K intersect {v_i.x>=0}| are strictly less
than |K|/2. The exact sector identity

    Q_j+Q_l=|K|-X_i+Y_i

then implies

    X_i>Y_i for every i.                              (4)

Suppose T were unbounded. Since it is a nonempty intersection of three
closed halfplanes, a nonzero recession direction exists: take a sequence
going to infinity, divide by its norm, and pass to a unit-vector limit in
the three inequalities. Such a direction cannot lie in any closed double
cone, because that cone's own bridge functional is positive on every
nonzero direction in it. It therefore belongs to an open unique cone.
Cyclically relabel it as e=(s,-u) in unique cone 1, with s>u>0.

Put alpha=B/A and beta=b/r. The first and third recession inequalities
give

    alpha<=u/s<=1-beta,

so alpha,beta>0 and alpha+beta<=1. Put ell=a/t and

    D_2=1-alpha+alpha ell>0,
    D_3=beta+(1-beta)ell>0.

Section 2 bounds the two OTHER actual unique sectors by the intersections
of their adjacent bridge halfplanes. The exact two-line quadrant-area
calculation, including collapsed additional vertices, gives

    X_2 <= [2Ba+B^2(1-ell)-at(1-alpha)]/(2D_2),
    X_3 <= [2ab-b^2(1-ell)-a^2(1-beta)]/(2D_3).         (5)

The complete determinant and endpoint feasibility calculation for these
same envelopes is Section 3 of
`candidate fd39a28eeb41e9c4`.
Only the two local bridge inequalities and the actual ray endpoints enter
that calculation. Section 2 above proves precisely those hypotheses here,
without assuming that any double sector is a core.

By (1),(4), the first right side in (5) must be strictly greater than
b^2/(2beta), and the second strictly greater than B^2/(2alpha). Multiply
by their respective positive denominators and add as in the explicit
square identity of the cited source. The result is

    0 > (B-beta t)^2/t + (b-alpha a)^2/a
                  +(1-alpha-beta)(beta t+alpha a),     (6)

which is impossible. Thus T is bounded.

It is therefore a triangle: it is the bounded intersection of three
halfplanes with zero strictly inside, and all three boundary lines contain
positive-length prescribed bridge segments. No inequality is redundant.
Its ray endpoints are exactly P_i, because it contains them and each lies
on a bridge boundary that excludes every farther point on its ray.

## 4. Exact sector comparison, including vertex-on-cut limits

In each double sector T has exactly its core triangle, by the corresponding
bridge support line. In each unique sector, (3) gives actual containment.
Consequently

    Y_i(T)<=Y_i(K),       X_i(K)<=X_i(T),               (7)

while all three full cutting sections are exactly the same.

The vertices of T belong to the respective CLOSED unique cones. To see
this, traverse the boundary of T from one double bridge segment to the
next. Its polar angle about the interior source increases continuously.
The intervening triangle vertex occurs between their adjacent ray points,
which bound exactly that unique cone. Thus no vertex is in a strict double
cone. A vertex may lie on a cutting ray; this is retained, not removed by a
general-position assumption. The three weak distinct-vertex incidences can
be approximated by strict incidences by moving each triangle vertex
slightly into its corresponding unique cone. Positivity of source interior,
caps, and full sections persists. Hence the proved strict-incidence triangle
Lorentz inequalities extend to T by continuity of its finite intersections
and areas.

**Sector-comparison theorem.** Every actual planar convex body with an
interior source and three balanced spanning through-source caps of area
strictly less than half its total area has a canonical triangle T with
exactly the same six ray endpoints. Its double sectors are the three core
triangles, and the original body's unique sectors are contained in the
corresponding unique sectors of T. Thus its exact raw data are obtained
from T's by nonnegative unique-sector losses and double-sector gains, with
all three sections fixed. T satisfies the triangle Lorentz inequalities,
including weak vertex-on-cut incidences.

## 5. A sufficient additional condition, and the remaining obstruction

If K and this T both have all three cap fractions at most 128/279, the
finite combined barrier proved in
`candidate c9c719c799483463`
applies to the exact transfers in (7). It gives all three rows of K at most
2, and all three strictly below 2 unless every sector area agrees. The
latter agreement forces K=T: each unique sector is a same-area convex
subset of T's, hence equals it; and each double sector contains its same-area
core triangle and hence equals that core.

The comparison triangle need not itself satisfy the cap ceiling, even when
K does. This condition cannot be omitted from the present barrier proof.
The theorem neither places K inside T globally nor claims to resolve that
remaining initial-ceiling obstruction. It also does not preserve any
mixed-fiber compatibility.

## 6. A two-stage path whose every sector array is actually realizable

The finite sector criterion supplies an additional geometric fact. With ray
endpoints held fixed, write c_i=1/(2W_i). The PSD matrix depends on them by

    L(c')-L(c)
       =sum_i (c'_i-c_i)(e_i+e_(i+1))(e_i+e_(i+1))^T. (8)

This follows directly from the exact defining form in
`candidate 2e26c63010f03ffc`: h_i is
the fixed constant 1/D_i minus c_i. In particular, reducing any collection
of sector areas, while leaving each at least its core area, preserves
positive semidefiniteness and hence actual convex-body realizability. The
new body has exactly the original prescribed ray endpoints; it is not
asserted to be a subset of the old body.

For the actual K and triangle T above, let W^0 have K's unique-sector areas
and T's double-core areas. This array is realizable: it is coordinatewise
no larger than K's actual array, so (8) applies. It is also obtained from
T's data by just the nonnegative unique losses in (7). The global cubic
loss theorem
`candidate b59c030c1c2567d0`
therefore proves its cubic bound without a cap ceiling.

Now vary each double-sector area between its core value in W^0 and its
final actual value in K, leaving all unique areas and all rays fixed.
Every intermediate array is coordinatewise no larger than K's actual
array and no smaller than the core array, and hence is realizable by (8).
Consequently this second stage is a finite continuous path of exact raw
data, each with an actual convex-body realization and the same full
sections. No continuous selection of realizing bodies is needed for that
assertion or for evaluating the continuous raw functionals.

Thus the remaining ordinary comparison problem can be isolated to actual
double-sector growth from an already cubic-feasible starting array. This
observation does not prove the desired derivative sign or that the cubic
bound survives that stage. It records exact geometric feasibility beyond
an unconstrained marginal-area relaxation.
